Our reality shows have held up a scalding mirror to our yapping baboon faces and cheesy, obvious obsessions, our trashy, gossipy love of trivia and dirt... I felt I’d really grasped the concept when I saw him as Everyman, or rather as the dreamself of Everyman. That emblem is the radiant symbol of divinity we reveal when we rip off our stuffy shirts, our social masks, our neuroses, our constructed selves, and become who we truly are. The brooding vigilante is obviously much cooler, but that’s because he’s a very energetic and adolescent fantasy character: a handsome billionaire playboy in black leather with a servant at his beck and call, better cars and gadgetry than a famous spy, a horde of dangerous women baying around his heels and no boss. That guy’s the hero day and night.

The alien hero grew up baling hay on a farm. He goes to work, for a boss, in an office. He pines after a hard–working gal. Only when he tears off his shirt does that heroic, ideal inner self come to life. That’s actually a much more adult fantasy than the one the vigilante’s peddling but it also makes the alien hero a little harder to sell. He’s much more of a working class superhero.

American writers often say they find it difficult to write the alien hero. They say he’s too powerful; you can’t give him problems. But the alien hero is a metaphor. For me, the alien hero has the same problems we do, but on a giant scale. If the alien hero walks the dog, he walks it around the asteroid belt because it can fly in space. When the alien hero’s relatives visit, they come from the future and bring some hellish monster conqueror from the future. But it’s still a story about your relatives visiting."
